## Introduction ### Learning goals Now that you know the basics of submitting and managing Slurm batch jobs, you will learn: - The most common Slurm/`sbatch` options, including those used to request: - More time, cores, and memory for jobs - An email notification when jobs e.g. fail or finish - How to run Slurm jobs in practice, including how to submit many jobs at the same time - How to make sure that your jobs succeeded - What to watch out for when using genAI to help with Slurm batch jobs - How to structure a multi-step workflow, and what workflow management systems and nf-core pipelines are ### Getting ready 1. At , start a VS Code session in `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER`. 2. In the terminal, navigate to your `week10` dir. ## Common Slurm/`sbatch` options In class, we'll go through the most commonly used `sbatch` options using the slides below (**[open them in a separate tab](./w10b_slurm-options.qmd){target="_blank"}** for a full-screen view). After that, you'll submit a job that exceeds its time limit. This section also has a reference table of these and some additional options, and a few more notes on cores, memory, and Slurm log files. ### Exceed the time limit ::: exercise #### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 3: Exceed the time limit 1. Modify your `scripts/sleep.sh` script from the previous lecture: - Reserve only 1 minute for the job - Make the script run for longer than that, by increasing the `sleep` time to at least 100 seconds When you exceed the time limit, an error message will be printed. **Before submitting the script**, predict the following: 2. Where will the error message be printed? a. To the screen b. In the Slurm log file c. In `sleep.txt` 3. Will `sleep.txt` and the "_I'm awake!_" line still be produced? a. Both will be produced b. `sleep.txt` will be produced, but the "_I'm awake!_" line will not c. The "_I'm awake!_" line will be produced, but `sleep.txt` will not d. Neither will be produced 4. Submit the script. The job will only be killed after a minute or two. Once the job is no longer in the `squeue` output, check whether your predictions were correct. ::: ### Table with `sbatch` options Here are the main options from the slides: | Resource/use | long option example | short option | default | | ------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------- | ------------ | :------------: | | Project to be billed | `--account=PAS3493` | `-A` | *N/A* | | Time limit | `--time=4:00:00` | `-t` | 1:00:00 | | Nr of cores | `--cpus-per-task=1` | `-c` | 1 | | Memory limit per node | `--mem=20G` | — | 4G per core | | Log output file | `--output=slurm-fastqc-%j.out` | `-o` | `slurm-%j.out` | | Get email when job fails
/ ends or fails | `--mail-type=FAIL`
`--mail-type=END,FAIL` | — | | : {.striped .hover tbl-colwidths="[25,40,15,20]"}
And some additional ones: | Resource/use | long option example | | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | | Put error output (*stderr*) into a separate file | `--error=slurm-fastqc-%j.err` | | Job name (will e.g. be displayed in `squeue` output) | `--job-name=fastqc` | | Partition (=queue type) | `--partition=longserial`
`--partition=hugemem` | | Only allow job to begin after a specific time | `--begin=2026-10-29T12:00:00` | | Only allow job to begin after another job has successfully finished | `--dependency=afterok:123456` | | Nr of nodes | `--nodes=1` | | Nr of "tasks" (processes) | `--ntasks=1` | | Nr of tasks per node | `--ntasks-per-node=1` | : {.striped .hover .smaller-table} For more about `--error`, `--partition`, and email warnings before a job hits its time limit, see the [optional self-study page on Slurm](../bonus/slurm.qmd#more-sbatch-options). ### Notes on cores, memory, and log files :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ##### What about nodes and tasks? _(Click to expand)_ You may wonder why the option is `--cpus-per-task` rather than just `--cpus`. Slurm can also reserve multiple **nodes** (`--nodes`) and multiple **tasks**, i.e. independent processes (`--ntasks`). Both default to 1, which is almost always what you want in bioinformatics: for example, multiple nodes are only useful for programs parallelized with "MPI", which is rare. With 1 node and 1 task, `--cpus-per-task` simply sets the number of cores. You may also see `--ntasks=n` being used for multi-threading, including in OSC's documentation: in practice, that also gives you `n` cores that a program can use. (Yes, this is confusing!) ::: ::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"} #### It is not always clear what happened when your job ran out of memory _(Click to expand)_ Whereas you get a very clear Slurm error message when you hit the time limit (as seen in Exercise 3), hitting the memory limit can result in a variety of errors. But look for keywords such as "Killed", "Out of Memory" / "OOM", and "Core Dumped", as well as actual "dumped cores" in your working dir (large files with names like `core.`, these can be deleted). If you see these or otherwise suspect that your job ran out of memory, resubmit it with an increased requested amount of memory. ::: ## Batch job examples with FastQC In week 7, we used a `for` loop to run FastQC for every FASTQ file, one after the other. This ran quickly, but keep in mind that our practice FASTQ files are only 5% of their original sizes. Additionally, other bioinformatics programs may take much longer, even for small files. To speed things up, and not block the terminal while programs are running, we will **submit a batch job for each sample/file**, so that many jobs can run simultaneously^[ But keep in mind that batch jobs are sometimes queued/waiting for a while, especially if you submit large amounts of jobs.]. So, let's practice with submitting a batch job for each FastQC run. We'll first submit a job for a single file, and then loop over all files to submit many jobs. You should have the FastQC script in `scripts/fastqc.sh`. ### Modify the script for usage with Slurm Here, you'll add Slurm options to the script with `#SBATCH` lines, and consider whether FastQC should use multiple cores. When you have multiple cores at your disposal in a batch job, you should almost always **explicitly tell the program how many cores it can use**. Some programs default to using 1 core while others try to auto-detect the number of cores, but any auto-detection tends to be inappropriate at OSC^[ The program is most likely to detect the _total_ number of cores on the OSC node, rather than the number we reserved.]. ::: exercise #### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 4: Add Slurm options to the FastQC script 1. Add `#SBATCH` lines to the top of `scripts/fastqc.sh`, so that: - The OSC project `PAS3493` will be billed - You'll get an email only if the job fails - The Slurm log file will be named `slurm-fastqc-.out` 2. Should you also reserve multiple cores for these FastQC batch jobs? Here is the description of FastQC's option for multi-threading, from its help info: ```bash-out-solo -t --threads Specifies the number of files which can be processed simultaneously. Each thread will be allocated 250MB of memory so you shouldn't run more threads than your available memory will cope with, and not more than 6 threads on a 32 bit machine ``` Given that each of our batch jobs will process a single FASTQ file, would, say, 4 cores and `--threads 4` make each job faster? ::: ### A single test batch job #### Submit the batch job Now, you're ready to submit the script. Let's test it for one sample first: ```bash sbatch scripts/fastqc.sh ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz results/fastqc ``` ```bash-out Submitted batch job 37615710 ``` #### Monitor the batch job Next, monitor your job by checking its status in the Slurm queue: ```bash squeue -u $USER -l ``` ```bash-out Wed Oct 28 14:31:48 2026 JOBID PARTITION NAME USER STATE TIME TIME_LIMI NODES NODELIST(REASON) 37615710 cpu-exp fastqc.s jelmer RUNNING 0:01 1:00:00 1 p0510 ``` After a while: - You will know that your job has stopped running (either due to failure or because it finished successfully) when it is no longer listed in the `squeue` output. - If you additionally didn't receive an email from Slurm, this suggests the job succeeded --- job failure should have triggered an email due to the `#SBATCH --mail-type=FAIL` line. #### Check the output files Even if you've inferred that your job succeeded from the abovementioned clues, don't forget to look at the output files to confirm this: - **Slurm log file**: The combination of having strict bash `set` settings and the "_Successfully finished_" `echo` line at the end of the script means that if you see that line printed, the script encountered no errors. Nevertheless, you should also look at the rest of this file, because a program's "logging statements" may have useful information, including output summaries but also warnings. - **The program's main output files**: As discussed, most bioinformatics tools don't just print "logging" information that ends up in the Slurm log file, but will also have output files (in the case of FastQC, an HTML and a Zip file). Therefore, always check the output dir for the presence of such output files. Check that the Slurm log file ends with the "marker" line that indicates a successful run: ```bash tail slurm-fastqc*.out ``` ```bash-out Approx 90% complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz Approx 95% complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz Approx 100% complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz Analysis complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz Used FastQC version: FastQC v0.12.1 Successfully finished script fastqc.sh Wed Oct 28 02:31:51 PM EDT 2026 ``` (With a real analysis, you'd also want to read through the whole file, e.g. with `less`.) ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} #### Optional: hide Apptainer's `INFO` messages in your Slurm log files _(Click to expand)_ When you run a program with `apptainer exec`, Apptainer prints some messages of its own, like "_INFO: gocryptfs not found, will not be able to use gocryptfs_". These are harmless, but clutter your Slurm log files. To hide them, add the `--quiet` option right after `apptainer` (warnings and errors will still be shown): ```{.file .bash filename="scripts/fastqc.sh (excerpt)"} apptainer --quiet exec "$CONTAINER" fastqc --outdir "$outdir" "$fastq" ```
::: Finally, check for the presence of the main FastQC output files: ```bash ls -lh results/fastqc ``` ```bash-out total 1.1M -rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 718K Oct 28 14:31 S63_R1_fastqc.html -rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 364K Oct 28 14:31 S63_R1_fastqc.zip ``` It can also be a good idea to pay attention to the sizes of output files, as shown by `ls -lh`. Especially if you're not going to open the output files right away, this can be yet another clue as to whether the program succeeded. When they fail, some programs produce empty or extremely small output files --- their presence should always be a red flag. #### Clean up Because this was a test-run, and you will now run a loop to analyze each sample, let's remove the outputs: ```bash rm -r results/fastqc slurm-fastqc* ``` ::: exercise #### {{< fa user-edit >}} Self-study exercise 1: Trigger a job failure email 1. Before trying it, predict what will happen if you submit `scripts/fastqc.sh` as a batch job **without any arguments**: - Will the `sbatch` command itself give you an error? - What error message will end up in the Slurm log file? - Will a `results/fastqc` dir be created?
{{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution_ - No: `sbatch` doesn't look at your script's arguments, so it will simply print `Submitted batch job `. The error only happens later, when the script runs inside the job. - Because of `set -u`, the script will stop at the line `fastq="$1"`, and the Slurm log file will contain an error like `/var/spool/slurmd/job37615711/slurm_script: line 11: $1: unbound variable`. (Slurm runs a copy of your script, which explains that odd path.) (The line number will depend on how many `#SBATCH` lines your script has.) - No: the script exits before it gets to the `mkdir -p` line.
2. Submit the script without arguments, and check your predictions. Then, wait for the failure email to arrive. (If it doesn't arrive within a few minutes, check the queue to make sure your job isn't still pending.) 3. Optional: if you prefer, set a "Rule" in Outlook so the Slurm emails will not go to your Inbox but to a specific folder for such emails. ::: ### Submit a job for each file Next, we'll loop over all FASTQ files to submit a job for each file. Though before you do so, let's do a "mock-run", just like you did in [GA4](/GA/GA4.qmd) --- if you preface the command with `echo`, the command will just be printed instead of executed. That can be really helpful with loops, e.g. to make sure you are looping over the files you want: ```bash for fastq_file in ../garrigos/fastq/*fastq.gz; do echo sbatch scripts/fastqc.sh "$fastq_file" results/fastqc done ``` ```bash-out sbatch scripts/fastqc.sh ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz results/fastqc sbatch scripts/fastqc.sh ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R2.fastq.gz results/fastqc sbatch scripts/fastqc.sh ../garrigos/fastq/S64_R1.fastq.gz results/fastqc sbatch scripts/fastqc.sh ../garrigos/fastq/S64_R2.fastq.gz results/fastqc sbatch scripts/fastqc.sh ../garrigos/fastq/S65_R1.fastq.gz results/fastqc sbatch scripts/fastqc.sh ../garrigos/fastq/S65_R2.fastq.gz results/fastqc # [...output truncated...] ``` That looked as expected, so now you can actually submit the batch jobs: ```bash for fastq_file in ../garrigos/fastq/*fastq.gz; do sbatch scripts/fastqc.sh "$fastq_file" results/fastqc done ``` ```bash-out Submitted batch job 37615718 Submitted batch job 37615719 Submitted batch job 37615720 Submitted batch job 37615721 Submitted batch job 37615722 Submitted batch job 37615723 # [...output truncated...] ``` All these jobs were submitted in very quick succession, and we got our prompt back. Check the queue: ```bash squeue -u $USER -l ``` ```bash-out Wed Oct 28 14:42:01 2026 JOBID PARTITION NAME USER STATE TIME TIME_LIMI NODES NODELIST(REASON) 37615718 cpu-exp fastqc.s jelmer RUNNING 0:03 1:00:00 1 p0840 37615719 cpu-exp fastqc.s jelmer RUNNING 0:03 1:00:00 1 p0840 37615720 cpu-exp fastqc.s jelmer RUNNING 0:03 1:00:00 1 p0840 37615721 cpu-exp fastqc.s jelmer RUNNING 0:03 1:00:00 1 p0840 37615722 cpu-exp fastqc.s jelmer RUNNING 0:03 1:00:00 1 p0840 37615723 cpu-exp fastqc.s jelmer RUNNING 0:03 1:00:00 1 p0840 37615724 cpu-exp fastqc.s jelmer RUNNING 0:03 1:00:00 1 p0840 37615725 cpu-exp fastqc.s jelmer RUNNING 0:03 1:00:00 1 p0840 # [...output truncated...] ``` Nice! At least in this case, all jobs started running simultaneously right away! Once all jobs have finished (are no longer listed in `squeue` output), you should have many Slurm log files: ```bash ls ``` 
results                    slurm-fastqc-37615719.out  slurm-fastqc-37615723.out  slurm-fastqc-37615727.out  slurm-fastqc-37615731.out  slurm-fastqc-37615735.out
scripts                    slurm-fastqc-37615720.out  slurm-fastqc-37615724.out  slurm-fastqc-37615728.out  slurm-fastqc-37615732.out  slurm-fastqc-37615736.out
slurm-fastqc-37615717.out  slurm-fastqc-37615721.out  slurm-fastqc-37615725.out  slurm-fastqc-37615729.out  slurm-fastqc-37615733.out  slurm-fastqc-37615737.out
slurm-fastqc-37615718.out  slurm-fastqc-37615722.out  slurm-fastqc-37615726.out  slurm-fastqc-37615730.out  slurm-fastqc-37615734.out  slurm-fastqc-37615738.out
You now arguably have too many Slurm log files to go through, so what to do next? Here's what I would generally recommend: 1. Take a close look at (at least) one Slurm log file: ```bash less slurm-fastqc-* # [output not shown] ``` ::: {.callout-tip} #### "Cycle" through files with `less` When you pass multiple files to `less`, like in the command above, it will only open one file at a time, but you can "cycle" through the files: as `less` itself suggests at the bottom of the screen, successively press : then n to go to the next file. ::: 2. Check the last few lines of all of them: ```bash tail slurm-fastqc-* ``` ```bash-out ==> slurm-fastqc-37615717.out <== Approx 85% complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz Approx 90% complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz Approx 95% complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz Approx 100% complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz Analysis complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz Used FastQC version: FastQC v0.12.1 Successfully finished script fastqc.sh Wed Oct 28 02:42:05 PM EDT 2026 ==> slurm-fastqc-37615718.out <== Approx 85% complete for S64_R1.fastq.gz Approx 90% complete for S64_R1.fastq.gz Approx 95% complete for S64_R1.fastq.gz Approx 100% complete for S64_R1.fastq.gz Analysis complete for S64_R1.fastq.gz Used FastQC version: FastQC v0.12.1 Successfully finished script fastqc.sh Wed Oct 28 02:42:13 PM EDT 2026 # [...output truncated...] ``` 3. Check for the presence of the FastQC output files: ```bash ls -lh results/fastqc ``` ```bash-out total 25M -rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 718K Oct 28 14:42 S63_R1_fastqc.html -rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 364K Oct 28 14:42 S63_R1_fastqc.zip -rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 714K Oct 28 14:42 S64_R1_fastqc.html -rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 366K Oct 28 14:42 S64_R1_fastqc.zip -rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 713K Oct 28 14:42 S65_R1_fastqc.html -rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 367K Oct 28 14:42 S65_R1_fastqc.zip -rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 718K Oct 28 14:42 S66_R1_fastqc.html -rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 372K Oct 28 14:42 S66_R1_fastqc.zip -rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 710K Oct 28 14:42 S67_R1_fastqc.html # [...output truncated...] ``` ::: exercise #### {{< fa user-edit >}} Self-study exercise 2: Check all jobs at once Scrolling through the `tail` output of 44 files is tedious, and it's easy to miss a failed job. Using a command you learned in week 4, how could you check, in one go: 1. Which Slurm log files have the "_Successfully finished_" line?
{{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution_ `grep -c` prints a count for each file when you give it multiple files, so any file with a count of `0` belongs to a job that didn't finish: ```bash grep -c "Successfully finished" slurm-fastqc-*.out ``` ```bash-out slurm-fastqc-37615718.out:1 slurm-fastqc-37615719.out:1 # [...output truncated...] ```
2. Whether FastQC produced an HTML file for each of the 44 FASTQ files?
{{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution_ Count the HTML files, and check that this is 44: ```bash ls results/fastqc/*html | wc -l ``` ```bash-out 44 ```
::: If everything looks good, and you are convinced that all jobs have finished successfully, all that is left is to clean up the Slurm log files. In this case, it is useful to **keep these files** around somewhere, as they contain information about our runs (when, which files, what version, etc.). But we want to move them out of our working dir. It often makes sense to store them in a subdir of the program's outdir, e.g.: ```bash mkdir results/fastqc/logs mv slurm-fastqc-* results/fastqc/logs/ ``` To avoid moving log files by hand, you can also make your script put a copy of its Slurm log file in the output dir: see [this section](../bonus/slurm.qmd#copying-the-slurm-log-file-to-the-output-dir) of the optional self-study page on Slurm. ### Recap: Making sure your jobs ran successfully To recap, here is an overview of basic strategies to monitor your batch jobs: - To see whether your job(s) have started, check the queue (with `squeue`) and/or check for Slurm log files (with `ls`). - Once the jobs are no longer listed in the queue, they will have finished: either successfully or because of an error. - When you've submitted many jobs that run the same script for different samples/files: - For at least one of the jobs, carefully read the full Slurm log file, and check other output files. - Check that no jobs have failed: via email when using `--mail-type=FAIL`, and/or by checking the `tail` of each log for messages like "Successfully finished script". - Check that you have the expected number of output files and that no files have size zero (run `ls -lh`). ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} #### Job monitoring tip: See output added to the Slurm log file in real time _(Click to expand)_ Text will be added to the Slurm log file in real time as the running script (or the program run by the script) outputs it. However, the output printed by commands like `cat` and `less` is static and not updated in real-time. Therefore, if you find yourself opening/printing the contents of the Slurm log file again and again to keep track of the job's progress, then instead **use `tail -f`**, which will "follow" the file and _will_ print new text as it's added to the Slurm log file: ```bash # See the last lines of the file, with new contents added in real time tail -f slurm-fastqc-37615717.out ``` _To exit the `tail -f` livestream, press Ctrl+C._ ::: ## Update your `CLAUDE.md` GenAI can help with Slurm in many ways: writing `#SBATCH` lines, writing loops to submit many jobs, and especially figuring out why a job failed from its Slurm log file. The `CLAUDE.md` you made in week 9 tells Claude that you haven't learned about batch jobs, and should therefore run programs with a single core. Copy it into your `week10` dir: ```bash cp ../week09/CLAUDE.md . ``` Then, remove that line from the "Computing infrastructure" section, and add a section like this one, so that Claude writes scripts that follow this week's conventions: ```{.markdown .file filename="CLAUDE.md (excerpt)"} ## Slurm batch jobs - We submit shell scripts as Slurm batch jobs with `sbatch` - Put `#SBATCH` lines directly below the shebang line, with at least: `--account=PAS3493`, `--output=slurm--%j.out`, and `--mail-type=FAIL` - If a program can use multiple cores, request them with `--cpus-per-task`, and set the program's cores/threads option to the same number - In the usage line of a script, use `sbatch` instead of `bash` - Don't submit jobs yourself: show me the `sbatch` command instead ``` ## Zooming out: workflows ### Multi-step workflows In a typical omics project (and likely in your final project for this course), you need to run multiple consecutive steps to process and analyze your data: you have a "**workflow**". So far, we have focused on running individual steps, like FastQC. How do you organize and run your workflow as a whole? Recall this RNA-seq workflow, going from raw reads to gene counts: ![](../img/rnaseq-wf-2.png){fig-align="center" width="60%" fig-alt="A diagram showing the steps in an RNA-seq analysis pipeline." .lightbox} As [discussed in week 2](../week02/w2a_project-org.qmd#three-types-of-documentation-files), it is a good idea to keep separate Markdown files for: - A "lab notebook" with **chronological entries** of everything you did, including mishaps and dead ends. - A "protocol" with the **final code in order of execution**, needed to rerun your project's entire computational work. ### A protocol example Here is a (hypothetical) protocol for the workflow above. Each step runs a single-step script that takes in- and output files as arguments, and is submitted as one or more batch jobs: ````{.markdown .file filename="protocol.md"} # RNA-seq analysis of _Culex pipiens_ - Author: Jane Doe - Date: 2026-10-28 - This was run at the Ohio Supercomputer Center (OSC) ## Set up: Set the input file paths ```bash fastq_dir=data/fastq ref_assembly=results/01_refseqs/assembly.fna ref_annotation=results/01_refseqs/annotation.gtf ``` ## Step 1: Read QC with FastQC `fastqc.sh` runs FastQC on 1 FASTQ file, and takes 2 arguments: the FASTQ file and the output dir. ```bash for fastq in "$fastq_dir"/*fastq.gz; do sbatch scripts/fastqc.sh "$fastq" results/fastqc done ``` ## Step 2: FastQC summary with MultiQC `multiqc.sh` runs MultiQC once for all FastQC outputs, and takes 2 arguments: the input dir (the FastQC output dir) and the output dir. ```bash sbatch scripts/multiqc.sh results/fastqc results/multiqc ``` ## Step 3: Read trimming with TrimGalore `trimgalore.sh` runs TrimGalore on the paired-end FASTQ files of 1 sample, and gives the output files the same names as the input files. It takes 3 arguments: the R1 FASTQ file, the R2 FASTQ file, and the output dir. ```bash for fastq_r1 in "$fastq_dir"/*_R1.fastq.gz; do fastq_r2=${fastq_r1/_R1/_R2} sbatch scripts/trimgalore.sh "$fastq_r1" "$fastq_r2" results/trimgalore done ``` ## Step 4: Alignment to a reference genome with STAR `star.sh` aligns the trimmed reads of 1 sample to the reference genome, and takes 4 arguments: the trimmed R1 and R2 FASTQ files, the reference genome FASTA file, and the output dir. ```bash for fastq_r1 in results/trimgalore/*_R1.fastq.gz; do fastq_r2=${fastq_r1/_R1/_R2} sbatch scripts/star.sh "$fastq_r1" "$fastq_r2" "$ref_assembly" results/star done ``` ## Step 5: Gene-level counting with Salmon `salmon.sh` counts the reads per gene for 1 sample, and takes 3 arguments: the BAM file from STAR, the reference annotation GTF file, and the output dir. ```bash for bam in results/star/*bam; do sbatch scripts/salmon.sh "$bam" "$ref_annotation" results/salmon done ``` ```` Structuring your workflow like this makes it relatively straightforward to rerun everything (e.g. with different samples or settings), or to reuse it in another project. And the protocol documents all steps that were taken. However, you **cannot** run all of this code at once:
Why can't all the code be run at once? _The answer will be added after class._
Which steps _can_ be run simultaneously? _The answer will be added after class._
### How about automation? There are two main ways to automate such a workflow further: 1. **With more advanced Bash and Slurm code**, e.g. by combining multiple steps into one script, or by using Slurm "job dependencies" so that jobs only start once the jobs they depend on have finished successfully^[ `--dependency=afterok:`, see the `sbatch` options table above.]. However, the added complexity of such scripts often doesn't pay off in the time you save (see [the optional Slurm self-study page](../bonus/slurm.qmd#automating-multi-step-workflows) for some examples). 2. **With a "workflow management system"**, which provides a way to formally describe and execute pipelines. The two most commonly used ones in bioinformatics are **[Nextflow {{< fa external-link >}}](https://www.nextflow.io/){target="_blank"}** [@ditommaso2017] and **[Snakemake {{< fa external-link >}}](https://snakemake.github.io/){target="_blank"}** [@molder_sustainable_2025]. These can e.g. automatically submit Slurm jobs, rerun only the steps affected by changes or failures, and run the same pipeline on different computers and datasets. Their main disadvantage is a somewhat steep learning curve. My recommendation is therefore to either: - Accept that your workflow isn't fully automated and use a Markdown protocol like the one above - Go all-in and use a workflow management system (specifically, Nextflow). The latter has become a lot more accessible with genAI, and is an **excellent use case for genAI**, because you can check it's work: if you already have a working protocol, you can run the genAI-written pipeline and compare its outputs to those of your protocol. ### Pre-existing pipelines Also keep in mind that you don't always have to build your own pipeline. Many publicly available pipelines exist, and Nextflow has by far the best ecosystem of these: the ["nf-core" initiative {{< fa external-link >}}](https://nf-co.re){target="_blank"} [@ewels2020] curates over 150 best-practice, flexible, and well-documented Nextflow pipelines, developed over years by many experts in the field. This saves you from having to figure out which of the many available tools and settings to use. Next week, we'll run the most widely used nf-core pipeline, the [rnaseq pipeline {{< fa external-link >}}](https://nf-co.re/rnaseq){target="_blank"}. ## Recap and what's next In this lecture, you've learned: - The most common `sbatch` options, to request time, cores, and memory, to name your Slurm log files, and to get emails when jobs fail - How to submit a batch job for each file with a loop - How to check that your batch jobs ran successfully - What to watch out for when using genAI to help with Slurm batch jobs - How to structure a multi-step workflow with a Markdown protocol, and what workflow management systems and nf-core pipelines are In [this week's exercises](w10_exercises.qmd), you will put all of this into practice with your TrimGalore script from GA4. Next week, you'll run an nf-core pipeline.
